big_idea: The specific words leaders use either reinforce top-down control behavior that silences good information, or unlock collaborative thinking and ownership across a team; leadership, Marquet argues, is best practiced as a deliberate discipline of language.

tool.label: Red Work / Blue Work
tool.text: Blue Work is thinking mode, planning, deciding, reflecting, debating options, while Red Work is doing mode, executing a plan with discipline. Marquet argues most organizations default to constant Red Work and treat thinking as a rare luxury, which drives people to plow ahead on flawed plans. His fix is deliberate, pre-planned pauses where a team shifts into Blue Work to reassess before resuming execution.

ideas.title: Six leadership plays for shifting language
ideas.text: Control the Clock (not obey it), Collaborate (not coerce), Commit (not comply), Complete (not continue), Improve (not prove), Connect (not conform).

ideas.title: Language of control vs. language of leadership
ideas.text: Phrases like I intend to replace passive, permission-seeking language and redistribute thinking and ownership downward.

ideas.title: Scaling questions over binary ones
ideas.text: Asking how confident are you, 1-10, instead of does this sound right surfaces real uncertainty a yes/no answer would hide.

ideas.title: Certainty is dangerous
ideas.text: Leaders who speak with excess confidence unintentionally shut down dissent and unwelcome information from their team.

ideas.title: The Red Work/Blue Work imbalance is an organizational design problem
ideas.text: Not just a personal communication habit, teams need built-in structures that force the pause.

ideas.title: Builds on Marquet's own submarine command experience
ideas.text: From his earlier book Turn the Ship Around!, extended here into a broader theory of workplace language.

try_it: In your next status update, replace I think we should maybe try X with I intend to do X and invite input before proceeding.
Add one scheduled pause point into a current project before the team moves to full execution.
Ask a team member a scaling question instead of a yes/no question in your next 1:1.
Notice one instance this week where you asked for compliance and reframe it as a request for commitment by explaining the why first.
best_for: Managers running technical or execution-heavy teams who want to reduce single-point-of-failure decision-making
Leaders who suspect their team is telling them what they want to hear
less_useful: Very small or already-flat teams where hierarchy isn't the bottleneck
Readers looking for quick one-liners rather than a systematic framework that takes practice to internalize

related.why: A complementary military-derived framework for decentralizing decisions under pressure
A related look at the specific leader behaviors that unlock, or shut down, a team's thinking
